catalog_quote: THE ACCENT. Generally dissyllables are accented on the first syllable, as: Mųca, long; pàtuk, wide; ūrur, a tree or log; ata, take; įi, call; gqmų, to bring or carry; mųni, stop stay, ūna, to wind; ūla, to unwind; mųna, to carry (as sticks on the shoulder); gįa to spear; ųcų, to hurl or shoot; ēna, a fly; ɛna, winter; cɛsi, summer, &c. Some are accented on the last syllable, thus: Up-puʃ, the sea egg, the burr of a plant; whilst upuʃ is wise; uzuʃ, a tree fungus. There are so many exceptions with respect to words of three or four syllables, that no rules can well be given, yet more frequently than not the accent is on the antepenult, as: Acupuʃata, to split through; Dągupataguna, to level out, spread out, to hold open or out; qnan cugqrata, there is a canoe on the water; qnan cucīsategeata, the canoe is pulled up on the beach; cupunaca, snow; belaca, rain; ēqʃu, to bark at, bring to bay…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Yámana (yama1264) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Guerra Eissmann 'Acento y sílaba en un corpus del Yagan' (Glottolog 79378, dated 1995), is confirmed by Dialnet (articulo 3293757) as Nueva Revista del Pacífico 38-39 (1993-1994, Homenaje a Félix Morales Pettorino), pp. 245-252, Spanish; it is about word stress in this language but no open copy exists anywhere checked (Dialnet record only; UPLA OJS archive and Dialnet full text start at no. 60/2014; SciELO from no. 64/2016; HathiTrust holds only nos. 7-16 of the journal, search-only; Google Books, OpenAlex, Crossref, archive.org: nothing). Priority high for print acquisition; note that Salas & Poblete and Aguilera 2000 reject Guerra's segmental analysis, so her accent analysis should be read against Salas & Poblete 1999 (RLA 37:107-122, also print-only). Read in this sweep from files already on file: Bridges 1894:54 (disyllables usually initial, some final; 3-4 syllable words mostly antepenult, no firm rule), Spegazzini 1884:135 (penult default, antepenult in longer consonant-final words; accent weakly perceptible), Aguilera 2000:238 (modern fieldwork: accent varies by context and shifts position; examples on initial, penult and final syllables). Best statement: Bridges 1894:54. all lookups were done by direct fetch of APIs and sites.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed stress position: two-syllable words are usually stressed on the first syllable but some lexically on the last (near-minimal pairs exist); in three- and four-syllable words stress is not rule-governed, with the antepenult the most frequent site. Bridges marks accent word by word in his orthography. Spegazzini 1884 (p. 135) independently reports accent as weak and hard to fix, 'generally penultimate' (= initial in disyllables) with antepenult in consonant-final polysyllables; Aguilera 2000 says the accent 'varía según el contexto, cambiando de posición en muchas ocasiones' and writes it with an acute on each example word.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables with final accent (Up-puʃ 'sea egg', uzuʃ 'tree fungus' vs ʉpuʃ 'wise'); polysyllables 'so many exceptions that no rules can well be given'. Spegazzini adds that suffixal endings such as -áta, -ánima, -ápata, -úpata carry the accent on their first vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (isolated words and short phrases in Bridges' examples); impressionistic, based on Bridges' c. 30 years of fluency in the Beagle Channel (Ushuaia) variety, 1860s-1880s. Modern phonological treatments of the last speakers' speech (Salas & Valencia 1990, Salas & Poblete 1999, Guerra Eissmann 1995 'Acento y sílaba') exist but could not be opened and may supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: Bridges 1894 describes Yahgan as he learned it at the Ushuaia mission on the Beagle Channel (1860s-1880s; usually taken as the central dialect); Spegazzini 1884 likewise worked at Ushuaia with mission-raised speakers. Aguilera 2000 (and the inaccessible Salas/Poblete/Guerra papers) describe the speech of the last speakers, Úrsula and Cristina Calderón of Ukika, Isla Navarino. All are the same language-level languoid yama1264 (ISO yag); no separate dialect glottocodes involved. Speakers reject the name 'yámana' in favour of 'yagán' (Aguilera 2000: 234).

new_statements.reading: Yahgan word accent has no exceptionless rule: disyllables are usually initial-stressed with lexical final-stress exceptions; longer words most often antepenultimate but with many exceptions. This is the only first-hand rule-shaped statement by a fluent speaker of the language. It is consistent in outline with Spegazzini 1884 (penult default, antepenult in longer consonant-final words) and with Aguilera 2000, whose modern data show accent 'varying by context, changing position' and whose examples spread over initial, penult and final positions. Net coding suggestion for a catalog entry: lexically variable / unpredictable stress with an initial (disyllable) or antepenultimate (longer word) tendency, sources Bridges 1894:54 and Aguilera 2000:238. Guerra Eissmann 1993-94 (NRP 38-39:245-252), the one title-keyword item, would be the dedicated study but is print-only and unread.

sources.citation: Spegazzini, Carlos. 1884. Apuntes filológicos sobre las lenguas de la Tierra del Fuego. Anales de la Sociedad Científica Argentina 18: 131-144 (section 'Del Alfabeto, del Acento y de la Pronunciación', pp. 134-136).
sources.quote: En la acentuación de la lengua Iákan no he podido determinar nada de fijo y constante, tanto mas que se nota muy poco en el discurso; [...] A pesar de esto se puede decir que por lo general el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba, ménos que en las palabras tri- ó poli-sílabas concluidas por consonante en las cuales entónces está acentuada la ante-penúltima. [transl.: In the accentuation of the Iákan (Yahgan) language I could not determine anything fixed and constant, all the more since it is little noticeable in speech; ... Nevertheless one can say that in general the accent falls on the penultimate syllable, except in tri- or polysyllabic words ending in a consonant, in which the antepenult is then accented.]
sources.note: Section 'Del Alfabeto, del Acento y de la Pronunciación', p. 135: 'En la acentuación de la lengua Iákan no he podido determinar nada de fijo y constante, tanto más que se nota muy poco en el discurso... A pesar de esto se puede decir que por lo general el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba, menos que en las palabras tri- o polisílabas concluidas por consonante en las cuales entonces está acentuada la antepenúltima.' (accent hard to pin down and weakly audible; generally penultimate, but antepenultimate in tri/polysyllables ending in a consonant; endings like -áta, -ánima, -ápata carry accent…

sources.quote: El mismo criterio de frecuencia se utilizó para la acentuación, ya que el acento varía según el contexto, cambiando de posición en muchas ocasiones. [transl.: The same frequency criterion was used for accentuation, since the accent varies according to context, changing position on many occasions.]
sources.locator: p. 238 (section 'Alfabeto oficial de la lengua'); accented forms throughout the phoneme lists pp. 235-240
sources.note: Modern fieldwork with the last speakers (Úrsula and Cristina Calderón, 1999-2000), explicitly corroborating Salas & Poblete. Word accent is mobile/context-dependent; the orthography marks the most frequent position. His accented examples show lexically varied placement: initial (péipi 'baby', ákis 'sea urchin', ánan 'canoe', wáfa, káluf), penult (estépa 'basket', ekóle 'one', kuluána 'grandmother', tumutúdu 'thunder', umasamái), final (amái 'chaura', taflá 'fat', axuá 'ash', iskín 'behind', uskú var. úsku 'smoke'). No positional rule is stated.

sources.note: Disyllables: generally initial stress, with some final-stressed exceptions (minimal pair up-púj 'sea egg' vs úpuf 'wise' implied by the contrast); 3-4 syllable words: too many exceptions for a rule, but antepenultimate more often than not. Author was a fluent speaker-missionary (32,000-entry dictionary); the fullest 19th-century first-hand statement.
